title: Magnetic Fields and Magnetic Field Lines
lead: A compass needle turns without anything touching it, and a magnet pulls a nail across a gap of air. Since magnetic forces act at a distance like this, we describe them with a magnetic field, and we draw that field as a set of magnetic field lines whose direction at any place is the direction the north end of a small compass points there. This section defines the field and its lines, shows the shape they take around a bar magnet, around a loop of current and around a long straight wire, gives the symbols for a field that runs out of or into the page, and ends with the four rules that every map of field lines obeys.
objectives: Define magnetic field and describe the magnetic field lines of various magnetic fields.
summary_html:
• Magnetic fields can be pictorially represented by magnetic field lines, the properties of which are as follows:
    1. The field is tangent to the magnetic field line.
    2. Field strength is proportional to the line density.
    3. Field lines cannot cross.
    4. Field lines are continuous loops.

figures.original_caption: Magnetic field lines are defined to have the direction that a small compass points when placed at a location. (a) If small compasses are used to map the magnetic field around a bar magnet, they will point in the directions shown: away from the north pole of the magnet, toward the south pole of the magnet. (Recall that the Earth’s north magnetic pole is really a south pole in terms of definitions of poles on a bar magnet.) (b) Connecting the arrows gives continuous magnetic field lines. The strength of the field is proportional to the closeness (or density) of the lines. (c) If the interior of the magnet could be probed, the field lines would be found to form continuous closed loops.

Small compasses could be used to map the fields shown here. (a) The magnetic field of a circular current loop is similar to that of a bar magnet. (b) A long and straight wire creates a field with magnetic field lines forming circular loops. (c) When the wire is in the plane of the paper, the field is perpendicular to the paper. Note that the symbols used for the field pointing inward (like the tail of an arrow) and the field pointing outward (like the tip of an arrow).

exercises.prompt: Explain why the magnetic field would not be unique (that is, not have a single value) at a point in space where magnetic field lines might cross. (Consider the direction of the field at such a point.)

answer.solution: The direction of the magnetic field at a point is the direction of the tangent to the field line through that point, which is the direction a small compass placed there points. If two field lines crossed at a point, there would be two tangents at that point and so two directions for the field, and a compass placed at the crossing would have two directions to point at once with no reason to choose between them. A compass in fact settles on one direction wherever it is placed, so the field has a single value at every point in space, and field lines therefore never cross.

exercises.prompt: List the ways in which magnetic field lines and electric field lines are similar. For example, the field direction is tangent to the line at any point in space. Also list the ways in which they differ. For example, electric force is parallel to electric field lines, whereas magnetic force on moving charges is perpendicular to magnetic field lines.

answer.solution: The two kinds of line are alike in most of what they do. The direction of the field is tangent to the line at any point in space, the strength of the field is proportional to how closely the lines are packed, lines of one kind never cross one another because the field has a single value at each point, and in both cases the lines are a pictorial tool rather than a physical thing, representing only the object that creates the field and not the probe that tests it. They differ in where they begin and end and in the direction of the force they describe. Electric field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges, while magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops with no beginning and no end, because a north pole and a south pole cannot be separated and no magnetic monopole has been found for a line to begin on. The electric force on a charge is parallel to the electric field lines, while the magnetic force on a moving charge is perpendicular to the magnetic field lines.

exercises.prompt: Noting that the magnetic field lines of a bar magnet resemble the electric field lines of a pair of equal and opposite charges, do you expect the magnetic field to rapidly decrease in strength with distance from the magnet? Is this consistent with your experience with magnets?

answer.solution: The two pictures resemble each other because a bar magnet's two poles are arranged like a pair of equal and opposite charges, so the field of the magnet should fall off with distance in the same way as the field of that pair. Far from a pair of equal and opposite charges the two fields very nearly cancel, and what is left falls off much faster than the field of either charge on its own, which the field lines say in their own way: they spread apart quickly as you move away from the pair, and the field is proportional to how closely they are packed. The magnetic field is therefore expected to weaken rapidly with distance, and this is exactly what handling magnets shows. A magnet on a refrigerator door holds firmly while it is touching, can be felt only faintly a centimeter away, and does nothing at all across the width of a hand.

exercises.prompt: Is the Earth’s magnetic field parallel to the ground at all locations? If not, where is it parallel to the surface? Is its strength the same at all locations? If not, where is it greatest?

answer.solution: The Earth's field is shaped like the field of a bar magnet lying inside the planet, and the lines of such a field leave the surface near one magnetic pole, arch out over the planet, and return to the surface near the other. The field is therefore not parallel to the ground everywhere. It is parallel to the surface near the magnetic equator, midway between the two magnetic poles, where the lines arch over horizontally; everywhere else it meets the ground at an angle, and near a magnetic pole it runs almost straight into the ground, which is why a compass needle free to tip as well as turn stands nearly on end there. The strength is not the same everywhere either. The lines gather together at the poles and spread apart over the equator, and since the strength of the field is proportional to how closely the lines are packed, the field is greatest near the magnetic poles and weakest near the magnetic equator.
